overview.text: The Dutch East India Company, known by its Dutch initials VOC, was founded in 1602 to organize Dutch commerce across Asia. Its charter gave it a monopoly on Dutch trade in a vast region and unusual powers to make treaties, build forts, hire soldiers, and wage war. The company traded spices, tea, coffee, textiles, and porcelain, while also using force to secure markets and territory. On Java it established Batavia, now Jakarta, as its Asian headquarters in 1619 after destroying the town then on the site. The VOC was therefore both a commercial enterprise and an agent of Dutch colonial expansion; its profits depended partly on coercion and exploitation.

key_facts.text: VOC stands for Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie, the Dutch East India Company.
The company was founded in 1602.
Its charter permitted treaties, forts, soldiers, and warfare.
Batavia on Java became the VOC’s Asian headquarters in 1619.
The VOC traded spices and other goods while using violence to enforce its position.

overview.text: Greece is a country in southeastern Europe at the southern end of the Balkan Peninsula. Its territory includes a mainland and many islands in the Aegean and Ionian seas, so the sea is a major part of its geography. Athens is the capital; the Cyclades lie in the Aegean, while the Ionian Islands lie west of the mainland. Greece is a parliamentary republic whose official language is Greek. It joined the European Communities, a predecessor of the European Union, in 1981 and now uses the euro. The name Greece refers to the modern state as well as the region associated with ancient Greek history, but its present political institutions are modern.

key_facts.text: Athens is the capital of Greece.
Greece occupies the southern Balkan Peninsula and has islands in the Aegean and Ionian seas.
Greek is the official language and the euro is the currency.
Greece joined the European Communities in 1981.
The Cyclades are an Aegean island group; the Ionian Islands lie west of the mainland.

overview.text: The Charge of the Light Brigade was a British cavalry attack at the Battle of Balaklava on 25 October 1854, during the Crimean War. Commander Lord Raglan wanted cavalry to stop Russian forces carrying away captured guns. Confusing orders and an obstructed view led the Light Brigade toward a different, heavily defended Russian battery. The riders advanced through artillery fire from the front and both sides; some reached the guns, but the brigade suffered severe losses and had to retreat. The episode became a symbol of courage amid command failure. Alfred, Lord Tennyson’s poem later helped make the charge one of the best-known events of the war.

key_facts.text: The charge occurred at Balaklava on 25 October 1854 during the Crimean War.
Lord Raglan’s order concerned guns captured by Russian forces.
The Light Brigade charged toward the wrong Russian guns after confused communication.
About 260 of the brigade’s 673 men were killed or wounded.
Tennyson wrote a poem about the charge.

overview.text: The Hanseatic League, or Hansa, grew from associations of northern European merchants into a powerful network of trading towns during the Middle Ages. Merchants joined together to protect journeys, secure privileges from rulers, and conduct long-distance trade around the Baltic and North seas. Lübeck became a leading Hanseatic city. Trading posts, called kontors, linked Hanse merchants to places such as Novgorod, Bruges, London, and Bergen. They exchanged products including textiles, metal goods, and Bergen stockfish. The league was a loose commercial alliance whose members negotiated common decisions and sometimes fought to defend trading rights; it was not a single kingdom with one ruler.

key_facts.text: The word Hanse originally referred to groups of traveling merchants.
Lübeck was a leading Hanseatic trading city.
Hanseatic kontors operated in Novgorod, Bruges, London, and Bergen.
Merchants joined to improve safety and gain trading privileges.
Bergen’s Hanseatic trading post was associated with stockfish.

overview.text: A chariot is a light, two-wheeled vehicle pulled by horses, used in several ancient societies for war, display, travel, and competition. Egyptian war chariots commonly carried a driver and a warrior, and the chariot corps was an elite part of the New Kingdom army. Other Egyptian examples were too light for battle and served different purposes. Images from Amarna show royal figures riding toward temples, while Greek athletic competitions included four-horse chariot races. Chariots therefore had no single function: their construction and use varied by place and occasion. The horse-drawn vehicle became a familiar symbol of royal and military power in ancient art.

key_facts.text: Ancient Egyptian chariots had two wheels, and war crews could include a driver and a warrior.
Egypt’s New Kingdom chariot corps was considered an elite unit.
Some surviving Egyptian chariots were too light for battle.
Amarna images show members of the royal family driving chariots to a temple.
Four-horse chariot races were part of the Panathenaic games at Athens.

overview.text: The Berlin Wall was a fortified border system built by East Germany around West Berlin beginning on 13 August 1961. The East German leadership sought to stop people leaving for the West through the city. Barbed wire soon gave way to walls and a wider strip of barriers, guards, and controlled crossings. The barrier separated neighbors and families; people attempting to escape were sometimes killed. Checkpoint Charlie became a famous crossing and a site of Cold War tension. On 9 November 1989, a mistaken announcement of new travel rules helped bring crowds to the crossings, which opened that night. Dismantling followed, and the Wall remains a symbol of Germany’s division.

key_facts.text: East Germany began sealing the border around West Berlin on 13 August 1961.
The Wall was intended to prevent departures from East Berlin to the West.
Checkpoint Charlie was a well-known crossing between East and West Berlin.
The crossings opened on 9 November 1989 after a mistaken travel-policy announcement.
The Wall included more than one concrete barrier and was gradually dismantled after opening.

overview.text: Constantinople was the city on the Bosporus that served as the capital of the Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire. Emperor Constantine established his new Roman capital at the older city of Byzantium in 330 CE, and it took his name. Its position linked the Black Sea region to the Mediterranean and placed it between Europe and Asia. Land walls, imperial buildings, and the great church of Hagia Sophia became landmarks of Byzantine Constantinople. Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II captured the city in 1453, and it then served as an Ottoman capital. Today the same city is Istanbul, whose historic districts preserve monuments from both imperial eras.

key_facts.text: Constantine established a capital at Byzantium in 330 CE and renamed it Constantinople.
Constantinople was the capital of the Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire.
Sultan Mehmed II captured the city in 1453.
After its capture in 1453, the city served as an Ottoman capital.
Hagia Sophia and the Theodosian walls are major surviving historic features.

overview.text: South Africa is a country at the southern end of the African continent. Its neighbors include Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and Eswatini; Lesotho is enclosed by South African territory. The country has nine provinces and a distinctive division of national functions among Pretoria, the administrative seat; Cape Town, where Parliament meets; and Bloemfontein, traditionally called the judicial capital. The Constitutional Court is in Johannesburg. For much of the twentieth century, apartheid laws enforced racial segregation and political exclusion. South Africa’s first national nonracial democratic elections were held in April 1994, and a new government took office in May. Its constitutional democracy recognizes many official languages.

key_facts.text: Lesotho is entirely surrounded by South African territory.
South Africa has nine provinces.
Pretoria is the administrative capital and Cape Town the legislative capital.
Bloemfontein is traditionally the judicial capital, while the Constitutional Court is in Johannesburg.
South Africa’s first nonracial democratic government took office on 10 May 1994.

overview.text: Hatshepsut was an Eighteenth-Dynasty ruler of ancient Egypt in the New Kingdom, reigning in the fifteenth century BCE. After the death of her husband Thutmose II, she first acted as regent for the young Thutmose III, then assumed the title and imagery of king while ruling alongside him. Her reign included building projects and renewed trade, including exchange with the land of Punt. Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri near Thebes remains a major monument. Objects bearing her names and royal titles show how she presented her authority. Some later monuments had her name and image erased; the reason for that campaign remains uncertain.

key_facts.text: Hatshepsut belonged to Egypt’s Dynasty 18 and ruled in the New Kingdom.
She first served as regent for Thutmose III, then became his senior co-ruler.
Her mortuary temple stood at Deir el-Bahri near Thebes.
Her reign included renewed trade with Punt.
Later erasure of her images occurred for reasons still uncertain.

overview.text: The Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, also called the Varus Battle, was a major Roman defeat in 9 CE. A coalition of Germanic warriors led by Arminius attacked a Roman army commanded by Publius Quinctilius Varus and destroyed three legions. Arminius had served with Roman forces, which helped him exploit Roman expectations and plan an ambush. The defeat disrupted Roman plans to control territory east of the Rhine. Archaeological finds near Kalkriese show a Roman-Germanic battle and support identifying that area as one site of the wider conflict, although the exact route and locations remain debated. The battle became an enduring reference point in Roman and later German history.

key_facts.text: The battle took place in 9 CE.
Arminius led Germanic forces against three Roman legions.
The Roman commander was Publius Quinctilius Varus.
The defeat interrupted Roman attempts to control lands between the Rhine and Elbe.
Kalkriese archaeological evidence supports, but does not prove every detail of, the battle’s location.
